knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 24-year-old previously healthy woman was admitted to the hospital with primary complaints of high-grade fever, generalized body ache, and decreased appetite for 5 days, followed by breathlessness for 1 day. Her vital signs on examination were as follows: pulse rate of 140 beats per minute, blood pressure of 110/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 60 breaths per minute, temperature of 38.4°C (101°F), and oxygen saturation of 60% on room air. Examination of the respiratory system revealed bilateral air entry without any adventitious sounds. Other systemic examinations showed no significant abnormalities. Laboratory results indicated thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 50,000 per cubic millimeter. Serological tests for dengue and malaria were negative.. Confirmed diagnosis: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome secondary to scrub typhus infection. Differential diagnosis includes: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome secondary to scrub typhus infection.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 63-year-old male with a history of smoking 23 pack-years, who quit 10 years ago, presented to the emergency room with difficulty breathing, 5 days after developing a widespread rash that began on his scalp. Upon admission, his physical examination revealed a fever of 38.5 °C, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 65% while on a high concentration mask at 15 L/min, bilateral rhonchi, cyanosis around the mouth and extremities, and signs of respiratory fatigue including paradoxical breathing. His blood pressure was 180/110 mmHg, heart rate was 110 beats per minute, and he had generalized papulovesicular lesions, some with necrotic centers. High flow nasal cannula therapy was started at 80 L/min with an oxygen inspiratory fraction of 100%, but there was no improvement, leading to the patient being intubated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by varicella pneumonia. Differential diagnosis includes: Acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by varicella pneumonia.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 49-year-old woman (89.9 kg, 167.1 cm, body mass index: 32.3 kg/m2) with no prior medical history, including heart failure, asthma, allergies, or reactions to iodinated radiocontrast material, visited the hospital for a self-paid medical imaging health check-up package. This package included MRI of the upper abdomen and low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) of the chest. The initial non-contrast LDCT of the chest showed no significant findings. Two hours after the LDCT, she underwent abdominal MRI following an injection of 15 mL (0.1 mL/kg body weight) of gadobutrol (Gadovist, Bayer Inc., Toronto, Canada). Ninety minutes post-injection, she experienced dyspnoea and cyanosis. Her vital signs were recorded as blood pressure 127/77 mmHg, pulse rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 35/min, and oxygen saturation 60% by pulse oximetry. In the emergency room, physical examination revealed diffuse wheezes and the use of accessory muscles for respiration.. Confirmed diagnosis: MRI contrast-induced acute respiratory distress syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: MRI contrast-induced acute respiratory distress syndrome.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A previously healthy, 59-year-old female was referred from Urgent Care for respiratory distress and dry cough lasting one week during the spring season. Outpatient chest radiographic findings indicated basilar pneumonia. She has a strong smoking history. She denied experiencing fever, chills, chest pain, orthopnea, sick contacts, and recent travel. Her oxygen saturation on room air was 95%, but she appeared diaphoretic and tremulous. Bilateral basilar crackles, more prominent on the left, with mild expiratory wheezing, were noted on auscultation. Initial chest X-ray showed a small left basilar airspace opacity. Initial blood work was within normal limits. She was administered high-dose intravenous (IV) steroids and antibiotics including vancomycin, levofloxacin, and piperacillin-tazobactam, and admitted for treatment. Within just over 24 hours of admission, her respiratory condition worsened. Arterial blood gas parameters were pH 7.44, pCO2 37 mmHg, pO2 63 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L, and FiO2 28. Oxygen saturation decreased to 88% on 2 liters per minute via nasal cannula. A repeat chest X-ray showed diffuse multifocal airspace opacities, and a lower extremity venous duplex
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Human Rhinovirus-induced Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 39-year-old man was admitted to the intensive care unit presenting with acute respiratory distress syndrome and renal failure. He required catecholamine therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and continuous renal replacement therapy. His condition had rapidly worsened within 2 weeks following a vacation in Turkey. Upon admission, laboratory results showed serum creatinine at 17.9 mg/dL, CRP at 17.7 mg/dL, and haemoglobin at 7.7 g/dL. Initial treatment included broad-spectrum antibiotics and antiviral therapy. Despite extensive investigations, no relevant infection was identified at the time of admission. Physical examination revealed moderate purpura on the skin.. Upon admission, his physical examination revealed a fever of 38.5 °C, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 65% while on a high concentration mask at 15 L/min, bilateral rhonchi, cyanosis around the mouth and extremities, and signs of respiratory fatigue including paradoxical breathing. High flow nasal cannula therapy was started at 80 L/min with an oxygen inspiratory fraction of 100%, but there was no improvement, leading to the patient being intubated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by varicella pneumonia. Differential diagnosis includes: Acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by varicella pneumonia.

This package included MRI of the upper abdomen and low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) of the chest. The initial non-contrast LDCT of the chest showed no significant findings. Two hours after the LDCT, she underwent abdominal MRI following an injection of 15 mL (0.1 mL/kg body weight) of gadobutrol (Gadovist, Bayer Inc., Toronto, Canada). Ninety minutes post-injection, she experienced dyspnoea and cyanosis. Her vital signs were recorded as blood pressure 127/77 mmHg, pulse rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 35/min, and oxygen saturation 60% by pulse oximetry. In the emergency room, physical examination revealed diffuse wheezes and the use of accessory muscles for respiration.. Confirmed diagnosis: MRI contrast-induced acute respiratory distress syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: MRI contrast-induced acute respiratory distress syndrome.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A previously healthy, 59-year-old female was referred from Urgent Care for respiratory distress and dry cough lasting one week during the spring season. Outpatient chest radiographic findings indicated basilar pneumonia. She has a strong smoking history. She denied experiencing fever, chills, chest pain, orthopnea, sick contacts, and recent travel. Her oxygen saturation on room air was 95%, but she appeared diaphoretic and tremulous. Bilateral basilar crackles, more prominent on the left, with mild expiratory wheezing, were noted on auscultation. Initial chest X-ray showed a small left basilar airspace opacity. Initial blood work was within normal limits. She was administered high-dose intravenous (IV) steroids and antibiotics including vancomycin, levofloxacin, and piperacillin-tazobactam, and admitted for treatment. Within just over 24 hours of admission, her respiratory condition worsened. Arterial blood gas parameters were pH 7.44, pCO2 37 mmHg, pO2 63 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L, and FiO2 28. Oxygen saturation decreased to 88% on 2 liters per minute via nasal cannula. A repeat chest X-ray showed diffuse multifocal airspace opacities, and a lower extremity venous duplex

tree.case_summary:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with complaints of a sore throat and difficulty breathing. His mother reports that the symptoms began the previous night and have worsened rapidly. The child is normally healthy, up to date on all childhood vaccinations, and takes a daily multivitamin. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 100/64 mmHg, pulse is 155/min, respirations are 29/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. On examination, he appears ill, is drooling, and leans forward to breathe. He is nonverbal, visibly uncomfortable, and does not cooperate with an oral examination. What is the most likely infectious cause of this patient’s symptoms?

Options:
A. Haemophilus influenzae
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae
C. Parainfluenza virus
D. Staphylococcus aureus
E. Group A Streptococcus
F. Adenovirus
G. Mycoplasma pneumoniae
H. Epstein-Barr virus
I. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
J. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)

excluded_candidates: Non-infectious causes of respiratory distress: reason ranked lower due to presence of high fever and sore throat
Cardiac causes of respiratory distress: reason ranked lower due to absence of reported cardiac symptoms
